\subsection{Trace Length Ablation}
\label{sec:trace_length}

A natural hypothesis for the 18.07pp gap between \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) and \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is that trace truncation discards diagnostic content: if the model saw more trace tokens, it might recover the missing signal.
We test this by training Qwen-2.5-7B under four trace token budgets: 256, 512, 1024, and no limit (the default \texttt{full\_trace} condition from Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).

\label{tab:trace_length}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:trace_length} shows that all four token budgets cluster within a narrow 77--82\% accuracy band, and the relationship is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) outperforms 1024 tokens (77.23\%), and the confidence intervals of all four conditions overlap substantially.
Critically, the no-limit condition---which retains the complete execution trace---achieves only 81.76\%, leaving an 18.07pp gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%; $p{<}0.0001$, paired bootstrap).
This gap cannot be attributed to truncation: even when the model has access to every trace token, it fails to extract the diagnostic signal that exception events provide directly.

The non-monotonic pattern further supports this interpretation.
If truncation were the primary bottleneck, accuracy should increase monotonically with token budget; instead, 1024 tokens performs 3.19pp \emph{below} 512 tokens (CIs: [74.87, 79.58] vs.\ [78.15, 82.61]), consistent with the information overload mechanism identified in \S\ref{sec:density}---additional trace tokens introduce noise that impedes rather than aids verdict prediction.
These results confirm that the \texttt{full\_trace} deficit is a signal quality problem, not a signal quantity problem: raw execution traces lack the information density of exception-based compression regardless of length.
